Make Any Photo Square in Seconds

Making an image square is essential for social media profiles, feed posts, and thumbnails. Unlike cropping, which cuts parts of your photo away, SquarePic makes an image square online by extending it with a blurred background, a solid color, or an automatic smart crop — so your full image stays visible. Use it as a free square image maker for Instagram, a photo resizer for any platform, or a quick way to keep an entire feed looking consistent.

1
Upload Your Image

Select any image from your device. SquarePic supports JPEG, PNG, WebP, and more. Files up to 20 MB.

2
Choose Your Style

Pick Dynamic Blur for a soft gradient background, Solid Fill for a clean color match, or Smart Crop to fill the square automatically.

3
Download & Share

Export your square image as PNG, JPEG, or WebP. Ready to upload to Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook, or any platform.

Three Ways to Make a Square Image
Dynamic Blur: Adds a blurred extension of your photo as the background. Creates a soft, professional look that Instagram influencers use for cohesive feeds.
Solid Fill: Adds a solid color background. Choose from preset colors or pick any custom color. Best for product photos and clean branding.
Smart Crop: Automatically crops the image to a square while keeping the most important content centered. No background extension needed.
Best Uses for Square Images
Instagram feed & posts: Square 1080x1080 posts display cleanly in the feed, grid, and profile — no surprise cropping on any device.
Profile pictures: Every social platform uses a square avatar. Make yours perfectly proportioned and centered.
LinkedIn & Facebook posts: Square images render fully in feeds on desktop and mobile, keeping your brand consistent.
E-commerce product photos: Amazon and Shopify both recommend square product images for clean, uniform listings.
Website thumbnails & favicons: Square thumbnails create tidy grid layouts, and favicons and app icons must be perfectly square.
Quote graphics & branded content: One square format keeps your entire feed or grid looking cohesive.
Social Media Square Size Quick Reference
Platform	Profile Picture	Square Post (1:1)	Best Format
Instagram	320x320	1080x1080	JPEG / PNG
Facebook	320x320	1080x1080	JPEG
LinkedIn	400x400	1200x1200	JPEG / PNG
X (Twitter)	400x400	1080x1080	JPEG
TikTok	200x200	1080x1080	JPEG
YouTube	800x800	1280x720	JPEG / PNG
Pinterest	200x200	1000x1500	JPEG / PNG
Snapchat	200x200	1080x1920	JPEG
WhatsApp	500x500	1080x1920	JPEG
Discord	512x512	960x540	JPEG / PNG
Why Make Images Square?

Square images (1:1 aspect ratio) are the most universally supported format across social media platforms. Unlike landscape or portrait images that get cropped differently on each platform, square images display consistently everywhere. Profile pictures are always square (even when displayed as circles), feed thumbnails are cropped to squares, and link previews often default to square aspect ratios. Using a dedicated square image maker ensures your photos look exactly as intended on every platform. Whether you need a quick square pic for your profile, a resizer tool for product images, or a full social media photo editor for your brand, SquarePic handles it all in one place.

Square Image Best Practices
Center your main subject — square cropping removes edges, not the middle.
Use high resolution source images (at least 1080x1080) for sharp results.
Match the blur background color to your brand palette for consistent social media aesthetics.
Add padding to prevent important content from touching the edges.
Preview your square image at actual size before posting to check readability.
Use the same square format across all profile pictures for brand consistency.
Check how your square image reads at thumbnail size — most posts are first seen small in a feed.
SquarePic also resizes, crops, compresses, and converts images — use the platform presets to prep any photo in seconds.
Private & Secure — No Uploads

SquarePic processes every image locally in your browser using HTML5 Canvas. Your photos never leave your device. No uploads, no servers, no data storage. This means you can edit sensitive images with complete privacy.

How to Convert Images Between Formats

Different platforms and use cases require different image formats. Whether you need a transparent PNG for a logo, a compressed JPEG for a website, or a modern WebP for better performance, knowing when to use each format makes a big difference.

Image Format Comparison
Format	Transparency	Compression	Best Use Case	Browser Support
JPEG	No	Lossy	Photography, web images, social media	Universal
PNG	Yes	Lossless	Logos, screenshots, graphics with text	Universal
WebP	Yes	Both	Modern web, performance-critical sites	97%
GIF	Yes	Lossless	Simple animations, memes	Universal
BMP	No	None	Legacy software, raw bitmap data	Universal
AVIF	Yes	Lossy + Lossless	Next-gen web, highest compression	93%
TIFF	Yes	Both	Print, publishing, professional photography	Limited
ICO	Yes	Lossless	Favicons, Windows icons	Universal
How to Choose the Right Image Format

Selecting the correct image format depends on your specific needs. Here is a simple decision framework:

Choose JPEG when:
You need the smallest file size for photographs
Universal compatibility is critical (email, social media, legacy systems)
Transparency is not required
Sending images via email or messaging apps
Choose PNG when:
You need transparency (logos, icons, overlays)
Maximum quality is required (screenshots, graphics with text)
Lossless compression is non-negotiable
Preparing images for further editing
Choose WebP when:
Website performance is the priority
You want JPEG quality at 25-35% smaller file sizes
You need both transparency and good compression
Your audience uses modern browsers (97%+ support)
Choose AVIF when:
Maximum compression is critical (50% smaller than JPEG)
You need HDR and wide color gamut support
Serving next-gen web experiences
You provide JPEG or WebP fallbacks for older browsers
When to Convert to JPEG

JPEG remains the gold standard for photographs and complex images on the web. Use JPEG when you need broad compatibility and small file sizes and do not require transparency. Most social media platforms recommend JPEG for photo uploads.

When to Convert to PNG

PNG is the go-to format for images that need transparency -- logos, icons, screenshots, and graphics with sharp text. PNG compression is lossless, so the image quality is preserved exactly. The trade-off is larger file sizes compared to JPEG.

When to Convert to WebP

WebP is Google's modern format that delivers JPEG-quality images at 25-35% smaller file sizes. It supports both lossy and lossless compression plus transparency. Use WebP for website hero images, thumbnails, and anywhere page speed matters.

When to Convert to AVIF

AVIF offers even better compression than WebP -- typically 50% smaller than JPEG at the same quality. It supports HDR and wide color gamut. Use AVIF for next-generation web performance, but always provide JPEG or WebP fallbacks for older browsers.

Batch Conversion Tips
Convert multiple images at once by uploading them all and setting the same output format.
Each file keeps its own quality slider -- adjust per image for fine-grained control.
Download all converted images as a single ZIP to save time.
Use the same output quality for batch jobs when all images are similar (e.g., same product photo set).
Format Selection Guide
Need transparency? Use PNG or WebP. JPEG does not support transparency.
Maximum compatibility? JPEG for photos, PNG for graphics. Both work everywhere.
Smallest file size? AVIF offers the best compression, followed by WebP.
Print quality? TIFF preserves the highest fidelity for professional printing workflows.
Animation needed? GIF works universally, but consider video formats for longer clips.
Favicon required? ICO format is the standard for browser favicons. Convert your 1:1 square PNG to ICO at multiple resolutions.
HDR content? AVIF supports HDR and wide color gamut (Rec. 2020), making it the best choice for modern displays.

Conversion Tips for Different Workflows
Web development: Convert all hero images to WebP with JPEG fallback via <picture> elements. This saves 25-35% bandwidth without changing visual quality.
Social media: JPEG at 85% quality is the sweet spot for Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter. PNG is unnecessary for photos and creates files 3-5x larger.
Email newsletters: Most email clients only support JPEG and PNG reliably. Convert WebP/AVIF images to JPEG before inserting them into email campaigns.
Game development: PNG for sprites and UI elements (lossless, transparency), JPEG for textures and backgrounds, WebP for packaging if engine supports it.
Archiving: Store original files in a lossless format (PNG or TIFF). Convert to lossy formats (JPEG, WebP) only for distribution to save space.
Understanding Quality Settings
100%: Near-lossless output. Suitable for archival or when maximum quality is critical. File sizes are largest.
80-95%: High quality for professional use. Great for photography portfolios and product images where quality matters most.
60-80%: The web sweet spot. Images look nearly identical to originals but file sizes are 50-80% smaller. Best for general web use.
40-60%: Good for thumbnails, previews, and placeholder images. Visible artifacts in smooth gradients but acceptable for small display sizes.
Below 40%: Heavy compression for extreme size reduction. Noticeable artifacts. Only use for previews, thumbnails, or bandwidth-critical applications.
Privacy-First Image Conversion

Every image conversion happens locally in your browser using HTML5 Canvas. Your images are never uploaded to any server.

How to Compress Images Like a Pro

Image compression reduces file size by removing redundant data while preserving visual quality. Smaller images load faster on websites, send quicker in emails, and take up less storage space.

Quality vs File Size

Higher quality retains more detail but creates larger files. For web use, quality 70-85% is ideal - images look nearly identical to originals but are 50–80% smaller. For thumbnails, quality 40-60% works well.

Target Size Mode

Need an image under 100 KB? Enable target size mode and set your goal. The compressor automatically adjusts the quality slider to hit your exact file size target, saving you manual trial and error.

Batch Compression

Compress multiple images at once to save time. Upload several files, set your quality or target size, and download them all as a ZIP archive. Each image is compressed individually for optimal results.

Lossy vs Lossless

JPEG compression is lossy -- some data is discarded to reduce size. PNG compression is lossless -- quality stays identical. WebP supports both modes. Choose based on whether you need perfect quality or smaller files.

Image Compression Format Comparison
Format	Compression	Best For	Typical Savings
JPEG	Lossy	Photos, web images	50–80%
PNG	Lossless	Screenshots, logos, graphics with text	10-40%
WebP	Lossy + Lossless	Web performance, modern sites	25-35% vs JPEG
When to Compress Images
Website performance: Compress hero images and product photos to improve Core Web Vitals and page load times.
Email attachments: Most email servers reject files over 25 MB. Compression keeps your images within limits.
Social media uploads: Platforms like Instagram and LinkedIn have file size caps. Pre-compress to ensure smooth uploads.
Cloud storage: Reduce backup sizes and save on storage costs by compressing images before archiving.
E-commerce product images: Compressed product photos load faster on shop pages, improving conversion rates and reducing bounce rates on mobile.
CMS and blog uploads: Most content management systems have upload limits. Pre-compress to avoid hitting file size caps and keep your media library lean.
Compression Best Practices
Always keep the original file as a backup before compressing.
Start at quality 80% and adjust down only if the file is still too large.
Use lossless compression (PNG) for screenshots and graphics with sharp text edges.
For website hero images, compress to under 200 KB for fast loading on mobile connections.
Batch compress before uploading to a content management system to save time.
Compress thumbnails aggressively (quality 40-50%) — they are small and fast loading matters most.
Re-compress previously optimized images only if you need even smaller files for a specific use case.
Common Compression Myths
Myth: Compression always ruins quality. Modern compression algorithms preserve visual quality down to 70-80% quality. The difference is often invisible to the human eye while cutting file sizes by more than half.
Myth: You should never compress PNG. PNG compression is lossless — file sizes shrink without any quality loss. Many PNG files have inefficient metadata and color profiles that can be stripped safely.
Myth: WebP always beats JPEG. WebP offers better compression at equivalent quality, but JPEG still wins for compatibility and is better for photographs with subtle gradients at high quality settings.
Myth: Compressing once is enough. Different platforms and use cases need different file sizes. An image for email should be smaller than one for print. Always compress for the specific medium.
Compression & SEO
Page speed is a confirmed Google ranking factor — compressed images load faster and improve user experience signals.
Core Web Vitals track Largest Contentful Paint — hero images that are compressed load before the 2.5-second threshold.
Google Lighthouse flags images that can be compressed further — passing this audit improves your SEO score.
Smaller images reduce bandwidth costs for your hosting and improve time-to-interactive for mobile visitors on slow networks.
Compression Targets by Use Case
Website hero images: Target under 200 KB at quality 80%. Use WebP format for best quality-to-size ratio.
Product photos: Compress to 100-300 KB each. Higher quality (85%) for zoomable images, lower for thumbnails.
Email attachments: Keep images under 500 KB. Most email clients block images over 5-10 MB total.
Social media uploads: Social platforms apply their own upload caps and compress images after upload. Pre-compress to 1-5 MB for fast uploads with the least quality loss.
Blog thumbnails: Compress aggressively to 30-50 KB at quality 60%. Small size matters more than perfection.
Quality Settings Guide
90-100%: Near-lossless. Use for archival, photography portfolios, and print-ready exports.
75-90%: Excellent quality for web. Images look identical to originals but 50-70% smaller. Best for hero images and product photos.
60-75%: Good quality for general web use. Visible only in side-by-side comparisons. Ideal for blog content and galleries.
40-60%: Acceptable for thumbnails and previews. Some artifacts visible in gradients and skies.
Below 40%: Heavy compression for extreme size reduction. Suitable for placeholder images, small thumbnails, and low-bandwidth scenarios.
Private & Secure Compression

All image compression happens locally in your browser using the Canvas API. Your files are never uploaded to any server.

How to Crop Images for Social Media

Cropping is one of the most fundamental image editing skills. The right crop can transform a mediocre composition into a striking image. Whether you are preparing images for Instagram, LinkedIn, or YouTube, choosing the correct aspect ratio is essential.

Precision Crop Controls

Our image cropper gives you eight drag handles for pixel-perfect control. Resize the crop area freely or lock the aspect ratio to maintain consistent dimensions across multiple images.

Aspect Ratio Lock

Keep your crop proportional with built-in presets for Instagram (1:1), portrait (4:5), widescreen (16:9), and story (9:16). The lock button toggles freeform mode for custom dimensions.

Zoom and Pan

Zoom in for detailed adjustments and pan around the image to position the crop area exactly where you want it. Fine-tune your composition without losing resolution.

Export at Full Resolution

The cropped image exports at the exact pixel dimensions you defined -- no downscaling. Download as JPEG, PNG, or WebP for maximum flexibility.

Aspect Ratio Quick Reference
Ratio	Common Dimensions	Best For	Platform
1:1	1080x1080	Profile photos, square posts	Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook
4:5	1080x1350	Portrait feed posts	Instagram, Pinterest
16:9	1920x1080	Landscape video, thumbnails	YouTube, Twitter/X
9:16	1080x1920	Stories, Reels, Shorts	Instagram, TikTok, YouTube
2:3	1200x1800	Portrait photography	Pinterest, print
3:2	1800x1200	Landscape photography	Blog posts, articles
21:9	2560x1080	Ultrawide banners	Twitter header, desktop wallpaper
Cropping Best Practices
Follow the rule of thirds -- position key subjects along the grid lines for balanced compositions.
Avoid cropping too tightly around faces. Leave some breathing room for social media rounded corners.
Use the same aspect ratio for a series of posts to create a cohesive feed aesthetic.
For print, always crop at the final output resolution to avoid quality loss from upscaling.
Check platform guidelines -- each social network has specific optimal image dimensions.
Common Cropping Mistakes
Cropping at joints: Avoid cutting off limbs at the ankle, wrist, or knee -- it looks unnatural.
Too much headroom: Leaving too much space above the subject makes the image feel empty.
Ignoring orientation: A vertical crop for a horizontal layout wastes pixels and looks awkward.
Over-cropping: Removing too much context can make the subject unrecognizable or the story unclear.
Cropping for Different Platforms
Instagram feed: Crop to 1:1 (1080x1080) for square posts or 4:5 (1080x1350) for portrait posts that fill more screen space.
Instagram Stories / Reels: Use 9:16 (1080x1920) full-screen vertical format. Keep text within the top and bottom safe zones.
YouTube thumbnails: Crop to 16:9 (1280x720) with bold, centered subjects. Thumbnails drive click-through rates.
LinkedIn banners: The cover photo is very short (1128x191). Crop tight and keep text in the safe center zone.
Facebook link previews: Open Graph images display at 1200x630 (1.91:1). Crop your images to this ratio for clean link shares.
Composition Techniques
Rule of thirds: Position key elements along the grid lines (or at their intersections) for naturally balanced compositions.
Leading lines: Use natural lines in your image (roads, fences, architecture) to draw the viewer's eye toward the subject.
Symmetry and patterns: Centered compositions with symmetrical elements create visually striking images that work well in square formats.
Negative space: Leaving empty space around your subject creates focus and gives text overlays room to breathe in social media graphics.
Fill the frame: Get close to your subject. A tight crop often creates more impact than a wide shot with too much background.
Crop Images Privately

All image cropping happens locally in your browser. Your images never leave your device.

How to Upscale Images Without Losing Quality

Image upscaling enlarges a photo while minimizing quality loss. Unlike simple browser zoom or stretching, our tool uses high-quality bicubic interpolation followed by smart sharpening to produce crisp, usable results at 2x, 3x, or 4x the original size.

Bicubic Interpolation

Bicubic interpolation produces smooth, high-quality enlargements by sampling 16 surrounding pixels (a 4x4 grid) for each output pixel. It preserves edge sharpness better than bilinear filtering while avoiding the blocky artifacts of nearest-neighbor scaling.

Smart Sharpen (Unsharp Mask)

After upscaling, a subtle unsharp mask is applied to enhance edge contrast and recover detail that naturally softens during enlargement. Adjust the toggle to control the effect.

2x, 3x & 4x Scaling

Choose from three common magnification factors. 2x is ideal for most use cases, 3x for aggressive enlargement, and 4x for extreme upscaling where maximum detail recovery is needed.

100% Private & Local

Every pixel stays on your device. The entire upscaling process runs in your browser using the Canvas API — nothing is uploaded to any server.

Upscale Factor Reference
Scale	Megapixels (1 MP input)	Example Input	Example Output
2x	4 MP	1080 × 720	2160 × 1440
3x	9 MP	1080 × 720	3240 × 2160
4x	16 MP	1080 × 720	4320 × 2880
When to Upscale Images
Print enlargement: Upscale low-resolution photos before printing to avoid pixelation at larger print sizes.
Social media covers: Enlarge small images to fit banner dimensions for Twitter, LinkedIn, or Facebook without stretching.
Product photos: Increase resolution of product images for e-commerce platforms that require high-resolution uploads.
Thumbnails to heroes: Convert small thumbnails into larger hero images for blog posts and landing pages.
Legacy photo restoration: Enlarge old digital photos to modern resolution standards before editing or sharing.
Website hero images: Upscale stock photos or small graphics to fit full-width hero sections on landing pages without quality loss.
Presentation slides: Increase resolution of embedded images before inserting into slide decks to avoid pixelation on projectors or large displays.
Digital art portfolios: Prepare artwork at higher resolutions for print-on-demand services that require minimum dimension thresholds.
Upscaling Best Practices
Start with the highest quality source image available. Garbage in, garbage out.
Use 2x upscaling for the best quality-to-size ratio. 4x is best for small source images.
Always keep the Smart Sharpen toggle on unless you prefer a softer look.
Export to PNG for maximum quality, or WebP for smaller files with good quality.
For best results, upscale images that are already sharp and well-exposed.
Understanding Upscaling Quality
Bicubic interpolation produces smoother results than bilinear or nearest-neighbor by sampling 16 surrounding pixels. It preserves edge definition better than simpler algorithms.
Smart Sharpen applies an unsharp mask after upscaling to enhance edge contrast. This recovers some of the perceived detail that naturally softens during enlargement.
Upscaling is not magic — it cannot create detail that is not in the original image. The best results come from sharp, well-exposed source images. Severely compressed or blurry originals will not look sharp after upscaling.
Source quality matters: A 500x500 image upscaled 4x to 2000x2000 will look significantly better if the original was saved at JPEG quality 95% versus 60%.
When Each Scale Factor Works Best
2x upscaling: Best quality-to-size ratio. Use for most general-purpose enlargements — profile pictures, social media posts, and blog images. Results are crisp with minimal softening.
3x upscaling: Good for moderate enlargement needs. Use when you need to convert small thumbnails to medium-sized display images or prepare images for half-page print layouts.
4x upscaling: Maximum enlargement for extreme cases. Best for converting tiny images for large displays, full-page print, or when the source image is very small and no alternative exists.
Private & Secure Upscaling

All image upscaling happens locally in your browser using GPU-accelerated bicubic interpolation. Your images never leave your device.

Why Image Dimensions Matter
Consistent Brand Appearance

Each social media platform displays images at specific dimensions. Using non-standard sizes forces platforms to crop, stretch, or letterbox your images, resulting in an inconsistent brand appearance. A 1080x1080 square image displays perfectly across Instagram, Facebook, and LinkedIn feeds.

Faster Page Load Times

Uploading images at the exact display size eliminates unnecessary data. A 4000x3000 photo scaled down to 400x300 in the browser wastes bandwidth and slows page loads. Use the calculator above to find the exact dimensions for each platform, then resize to match.

Aspect Ratio Explained

Aspect ratio describes the proportional relationship between width and height (e.g., 1:1 for square, 16:9 for widescreen). Two images with different pixel dimensions can share the same aspect ratio. Use our calculator to find which platform presets match your image's aspect ratio.

Avoid Upscaling Issues

Starting with an image that is smaller than the target dimensions means the platform must upscale it, causing blurriness and pixelation. Always upload images at or above the platform's recommended resolution. Our dimension calculator shows you the minimum size for each media type.

How to Use the Image Size Calculator
Search by dimensions: Enter your image's width and height in pixels. The calculator instantly checks if these dimensions match any standard social media image size.
Browse by platform: Select a platform from the buttons above to see all supported image sizes for that platform, from profile pictures to cover photos and post dimensions.
Click through to resize: Once you find your target dimensions, click any result to open SquarePic's resizer with the exact preset applied.
Common pairings: 1080x1080 (Instagram square), 1080x1920 (Instagram Stories), 1200x630 (Facebook link preview), 1280x720 (YouTube thumbnail) -- these are among the most frequently searched dimension pairs.
Common Image Dimension Questions
What is the most common image size for social media?

1080 x 1080 pixels (1:1 square) is the most universally supported size. Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and X/Twitter all display square images natively. It is the safest choice for cross-platform posting.

How do I calculate aspect ratio from width and height?

Divide both width and height by their greatest common divisor. For example, 1920x1080 simplifies to 16:9 (1920/120 = 16, 1080/120 = 9). Use this calculator to find which standard aspect ratio matches your image dimensions.

What resolution is best for print vs web?

For web, 72 DPI is standard and 1920px on the longest side is sufficient for most displays. For print, 300 DPI is required. Use the dimensions above as a starting point and always verify with your specific platform's requirements before uploading.

Instagram Image Sizes: Complete Dimensions Guide

Instagram image sizes for posts, stories, profiles, and reels. Square posts are 1080x1080, portrait is 1080x1350, landscape is 1080x566.

320X320
1080X566
1080X1350
1080X1080
1080X1920
All Instagram Image Sizes
Profile Picture: 320 x 320 px

Aspect ratio: 1:1

Centering the subject in the square crop matters more than background detail.

Landscape Post: 1080 x 566 px

Aspect ratio: 1.91:1

Great for showing wide scenes like landscapes, cityscapes, and group shots.

Portrait Post: 1080 x 1350 px

Aspect ratio: 4:5

The most engaging format for Instagram feed. Takes up more vertical screen space.

Square Post: 1080 x 1080 px

Aspect ratio: 1:1

The classic Instagram format. Works well for all content types.

Stories: 1080 x 1920 px

Aspect ratio: 9:16

Leave 250px top and bottom clear of critical content for the safe zone.

Frequently Asked Questions
What is the standard image size for Instagram?

Instagram supports multiple image formats. The most common sizes are 320x320 pixels, 1080x566 pixels, 1080x1350 pixels. Use SquarePic to resize your photos to any of these exact dimensions.

How do I resize images for Instagram without cropping?

Use SquarePic's free image resizer. Upload your photo, select the Instagram preset that matches your needs, and choose Dynamic Blur or Solid Background mode to fill any empty space without cropping your original image.

Is Instagram image resizing free?

Yes. SquarePic is completely free with no signup required. All image processing happens locally in your browser using HTML5 Canvas. Your photos are never uploaded to any server.

What is the best image format for Instagram?

For Instagram, JPEG is best for photos with smooth gradients, PNG is ideal for graphics with text or sharp edges, and WebP offers excellent quality at smaller file sizes. SquarePic supports all three formats for export.

Can I create a Instagram profile picture with SquarePic?

Yes. Upload your photo to SquarePic and use our free editor to make it perfectly square. Choose the Instagram preset size and export a high-quality profile picture in seconds.

Best Practices for Instagram Images
Recommended Formats

JPEG is the standard for Instagram uploads. PNG preserves quality for graphics with text. WebP is supported but not recommended for maximum compatibility.

Quick Facts

Instagram applies its own compression to every upload and crops feed images to square thumbnails. Matching the recommended dimensions keeps your full image visible and avoids avoidable quality loss.

Upload Tips

Post consistently at 1080x1080 or 1080x1350 for feed posts. Use 1080x1920 for Stories and Reels. Avoid compressed artifacts by uploading the highest quality version within Instagram's 20 MB limit.

Why Dimensions Matter

Instagram crops images in feed to square thumbnails by default. Using the correct dimensions ensures your full image appears without unexpected cropping. Portrait 4:5 posts take up more vertical screen space than squares, giving your content more visibility.

About PNG and AVIF Formats
PNG

Portable Network Graphics - lossless format with transparency support.

Best for: Logos, screenshots, graphics with sharp text and transparency.· Supports transparency· Lossless

AVIF

AV1 Image Format - next-gen format with 50% better compression than JPEG.

Best for: Next-gen web performance, HDR content, highest compression needs.· Supports transparency· Lossy compression

Tips for Converting PNG to AVIF
AVIF offers 50% better compression than JPEG at the same quality level.
AVIF supports HDR, wide color gamut, and transparency.
Browser support is at 93% - provide a JPEG or WebP fallback for older browsers.
AVIF is ideal for serving high-quality images on modern browsers while minimizing bandwidth usage.
When to Convert PNG to AVIF
Next-generation image compression

PNG to AVIF conversion delivers 50% better compression than JPEG while maintaining transparency support. It is the most efficient format for modern websites targeting the best possible performance.

Who needs this: Forward-thinking web developers and performance teams building next-gen web experiences.

Make Any Photo Square in Seconds

Making an image square is essential for social media profiles, feed posts, and thumbnails. Unlike cropping, which cuts parts of your photo away, SquarePic makes an image square online by extending it with a blurred background, a solid color, or an automatic smart crop — so your full image stays visible. Use it as a free square image maker for Instagram, a photo resizer for any platform, or a quick way to keep an entire feed looking consistent.

1
Upload Your Image

Select any image from your device. SquarePic supports JPEG, PNG, WebP, and more. Files up to 20 MB.

2
Choose Your Style

Pick Dynamic Blur for a soft gradient background, Solid Fill for a clean color match, or Smart Crop to fill the square automatically.

3
Download & Share

Export your square image as PNG, JPEG, or WebP. Ready to upload to Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook, or any platform.

Three Ways to Make a Square Image
Dynamic Blur: Adds a blurred extension of your photo as the background. Creates a soft, professional look that Instagram influencers use for cohesive feeds.
Solid Fill: Adds a solid color background. Choose from preset colors or pick any custom color. Best for product photos and clean branding.
Smart Crop: Automatically crops the image to a square while keeping the most important content centered. No background extension needed.
Best Uses for Square Images
Instagram feed & posts: Square 1080x1080 posts display cleanly in the feed, grid, and profile — no surprise cropping on any device.
Profile pictures: Every social platform uses a square avatar. Make yours perfectly proportioned and centered.
LinkedIn & Facebook posts: Square images render fully in feeds on desktop and mobile, keeping your brand consistent.
E-commerce product photos: Amazon and Shopify both recommend square product images for clean, uniform listings.
Website thumbnails & favicons: Square thumbnails create tidy grid layouts, and favicons and app icons must be perfectly square.
Quote graphics & branded content: One square format keeps your entire feed or grid looking cohesive.
Social Media Square Size Quick Reference
Platform	Profile Picture	Square Post (1:1)	Best Format
Instagram	320x320	1080x1080	JPEG / PNG

Snapchat	200x200	1080x1920	JPEG
WhatsApp	500x500	1080x1920	JPEG
Discord	512x512	960x540	JPEG / PNG
Why Make Images Square?

Square images (1:1 aspect ratio) are the most universally supported format across social media platforms. Unlike landscape or portrait images that get cropped differently on each platform, square images display consistently everywhere. Profile pictures are always square (even when displayed as circles), feed thumbnails are cropped to squares, and link previews often default to square aspect ratios. Using a dedicated square image maker ensures your photos look exactly as intended on every platform. Whether you need a quick square pic for your profile, a resizer tool for product images, or a full social media photo editor for your brand, SquarePic handles it all in one place.

Square Image Best Practices
Center your main subject — square cropping removes edges, not the middle.
Use high resolution source images (at least 1080x1080) for sharp results.
Match the blur background color to your brand palette for consistent social media aesthetics.
Add padding to prevent important content from touching the edges.
Preview your square image at actual size before posting to check readability.
Use the same square format across all profile pictures for brand consistency.
Check how your square image reads at thumbnail size — most posts are first seen small in a feed.
SquarePic also resizes, crops, compresses, and converts images — use the platform presets to prep any photo in seconds.
Private & Secure — No Uploads

SquarePic processes every image locally in your browser using HTML5 Canvas. Your photos never leave your device. No uploads, no servers, no data storage. This means you can edit sensitive images with complete privacy.

How to Convert Images Between Formats

Different platforms and use cases require different image formats. Whether you need a transparent PNG for a logo, a compressed JPEG for a website, or a modern WebP for better performance, knowing when to use each format makes a big difference.

Image Format Comparison
Format	Transparency	Compression	Best Use Case	Browser Support
JPEG	No	Lossy	Photography, web images, social media	Universal
PNG	Yes	Lossless	Logos, screenshots, graphics with text	Universal
WebP	Yes	Both	Modern web, performance-critical sites	97%
GIF	Yes	Lossless	Simple animations, memes	Universal
BMP	No	None	Legacy software, raw bitmap data	Universal
AVIF	Yes	Lossy + Lossless	Next-gen web, highest compression	93%
TIFF	Yes	Both	Print, publishing, professional photography	Limited
ICO	Yes	Lossless	Favicons, Windows icons	Universal
How to Choose the Right Image Format

Selecting the correct image format depends on your specific needs. Here is a simple decision framework:

Choose JPEG when:
You need the smallest file size for photographs
Universal compatibility is critical (email, social media, legacy systems)
Transparency is not required
Sending images via email or messaging apps
Choose PNG when:
You need transparency (logos, icons, overlays)
Maximum quality is required (screenshots, graphics with text)
Lossless compression is non-negotiable
Preparing images for further editing
Choose WebP when:
Website performance is the priority
You want JPEG quality at 25-35% smaller file sizes
You need both transparency and good compression
Your audience uses modern browsers (97%+ support)
Choose AVIF when:
Maximum compression is critical (50% smaller than JPEG)
You need HDR and wide color gamut support
Serving next-gen web experiences
You provide JPEG or WebP fallbacks for older browsers
When to Convert to JPEG

JPEG remains the gold standard for photographs and complex images on the web. Use JPEG when you need broad compatibility and small file sizes and do not require transparency. Most social media platforms recommend JPEG for photo uploads.

When to Convert to PNG

PNG is the go-to format for images that need transparency -- logos, icons, screenshots, and graphics with sharp text. PNG compression is lossless, so the image quality is preserved exactly. The trade-off is larger file sizes compared to JPEG.

When to Convert to WebP

WebP is Google's modern format that delivers JPEG-quality images at 25-35% smaller file sizes. It supports both lossy and lossless compression plus transparency. Use WebP for website hero images, thumbnails, and anywhere page speed matters.

When to Convert to AVIF

AVIF offers even better compression than WebP -- typically 50% smaller than JPEG at the same quality. It supports HDR and wide color gamut. Use AVIF for next-generation web performance, but always provide JPEG or WebP fallbacks for older browsers.

Batch Conversion Tips
Convert multiple images at once by uploading them all and setting the same output format.
Each file keeps its own quality slider -- adjust per image for fine-grained control.
Download all converted images as a single ZIP to save time.
Use the same output quality for batch jobs when all images are similar (e.g., same product photo set).
Format Selection Guide
Need transparency? Use PNG or WebP. JPEG does not support transparency.
Maximum compatibility? JPEG for photos, PNG for graphics. Both work everywhere.
Smallest file size? AVIF offers the best compression, followed by WebP.
Print quality? TIFF preserves the highest fidelity for professional printing workflows.
Animation needed? GIF works universally, but consider video formats for longer clips.
Favicon required? ICO format is the standard for browser favicons. Convert your 1:1 square PNG to ICO at multiple resolutions.
HDR content? AVIF supports HDR and wide color gamut (Rec. 2020), making it the best choice for modern displays.

Conversion Tips for Different Workflows
Web development: Convert all hero images to WebP with JPEG fallback via <picture> elements. This saves 25-35% bandwidth without changing visual quality.
Social media: JPEG at 85% quality is the sweet spot for Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter. PNG is unnecessary for photos and creates files 3-5x larger.
Email newsletters: Most email clients only support JPEG and PNG reliably. Convert WebP/AVIF images to JPEG before inserting them into email campaigns.
Game development: PNG for sprites and UI elements (lossless, transparency), JPEG for textures and backgrounds, WebP for packaging if engine supports it.
Archiving: Store original files in a lossless format (PNG or TIFF). Convert to lossy formats (JPEG, WebP) only for distribution to save space.
Understanding Quality Settings
100%: Near-lossless output. Suitable for archival or when maximum quality is critical. File sizes are largest.
80-95%: High quality for professional use. Great for photography portfolios and product images where quality matters most.
60-80%: The web sweet spot. Images look nearly identical to originals but file sizes are 50-80% smaller. Best for general web use.
40-60%: Good for thumbnails, previews, and placeholder images. Visible artifacts in smooth gradients but acceptable for small display sizes.

Free Image Compressor

Compress JPG, PNG, and WebP images online without losing quality. Reduce file sizes for faster website loading and easier sharing.

Drop images here or click to browse

Max 30MB per file

More Free Image Tools

Crop, convert, compress & resize - all in your browser.

Image Converter

JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF

Image Compressor

Reduce file size, batch

Image Cropper

Free-form & preset ratios

HD Image Upscaler

2x, 3x, 4x magnification

How to Compress Images Like a Pro

Image compression reduces file size by removing redundant data while preserving visual quality. Smaller images load faster on websites, send quicker in emails, and take up less storage space.

Quality vs File Size

Higher quality retains more detail but creates larger files. For web use, quality 70-85% is ideal - images look nearly identical to originals but are 50–80% smaller. For thumbnails, quality 40-60% works well.

Target Size Mode

Need an image under 100 KB? Enable target size mode and set your goal. The compressor automatically adjusts the quality slider to hit your exact file size target, saving you manual trial and error.

Batch Compression

Compress multiple images at once to save time. Upload several files, set your quality or target size, and download them all as a ZIP archive. Each image is compressed individually for optimal results.

Lossy vs Lossless

JPEG compression is lossy -- some data is discarded to reduce size. PNG compression is lossless -- quality stays identical. WebP supports both modes. Choose based on whether you need perfect quality or smaller files.

Image Compression Format Comparison
Format	Compression	Best For	Typical Savings
JPEG	Lossy	Photos, web images	50–80%
PNG	Lossless	Screenshots, logos, graphics with text	10-40%
WebP	Lossy + Lossless	Web performance, modern sites	25-35% vs JPEG
When to Compress Images
Website performance: Compress hero images and product photos to improve Core Web Vitals and page load times.
Email attachments: Most email servers reject files over 25 MB. Compression keeps your images within limits.
Social media uploads: Platforms like Instagram and LinkedIn have file size caps. Pre-compress to ensure smooth uploads.
Cloud storage: Reduce backup sizes and save on storage costs by compressing images before archiving.
E-commerce product images: Compressed product photos load faster on shop pages, improving conversion rates and reducing bounce rates on mobile.
CMS and blog uploads: Most content management systems have upload limits. Pre-compress to avoid hitting file size caps and keep your media library lean.
Compression Best Practices
Always keep the original file as a backup before compressing.
Start at quality 80% and adjust down only if the file is still too large.
Use lossless compression (PNG) for screenshots and graphics with sharp text edges.
For website hero images, compress to under 200 KB for fast loading on mobile connections.
Batch compress before uploading to a content management system to save time.
Compress thumbnails aggressively (quality 40-50%) — they are small and fast loading matters most.
Re-compress previously optimized images only if you need even smaller files for a specific use case.
Common Compression Myths
Myth: Compression always ruins quality. Modern compression algorithms preserve visual quality down to 70-80% quality. The difference is often invisible to the human eye while cutting file sizes by more than half.
Myth: You should never compress PNG. PNG compression is lossless — file sizes shrink without any quality loss. Many PNG files have inefficient metadata and color profiles that can be stripped safely.
Myth: WebP always beats JPEG. WebP offers better compression at equivalent quality, but JPEG still wins for compatibility and is better for photographs with subtle gradients at high quality settings.
Myth: Compressing once is enough. Different platforms and use cases need different file sizes. An image for email should be smaller than one for print. Always compress for the specific medium.
Compression & SEO
Page speed is a confirmed Google ranking factor — compressed images load faster and improve user experience signals.
Core Web Vitals track Largest Contentful Paint — hero images that are compressed load before the 2.5-second threshold.
Google Lighthouse flags images that can be compressed further — passing this audit improves your SEO score.
Smaller images reduce bandwidth costs for your hosting and improve time-to-interactive for mobile visitors on slow networks.
Compression Targets by Use Case
Website hero images: Target under 200 KB at quality 80%. Use WebP format for best quality-to-size ratio.
Product photos: Compress to 100-300 KB each. Higher quality (85%) for zoomable images, lower for thumbnails.
Email attachments: Keep images under 500 KB. Most email clients block images over 5-10 MB total.
Social media uploads: Social platforms apply their own upload caps and compress images after upload. Pre-compress to 1-5 MB for fast uploads with the least quality loss.
Blog thumbnails: Compress aggressively to 30-50 KB at quality 60%. Small size matters more than perfection.
Quality Settings Guide
90-100%: Near-lossless. Use for archival, photography portfolios, and print-ready exports.
75-90%: Excellent quality for web. Images look identical to originals but 50-70% smaller. Best for hero images and product photos.
60-75%: Good quality for general web use. Visible only in side-by-side comparisons. Ideal for blog content and galleries.
40-60%: Acceptable for thumbnails and previews. Some artifacts visible in gradients and skies.
Below 40%: Heavy compression for extreme size reduction. Suitable for placeholder images, small thumbnails, and low-bandwidth scenarios.
Private & Secure Compression

All image compression happens locally in your browser using the Canvas API. Your files are never uploaded to any server.

How to Crop Images for Social Media

Cropping is one of the most fundamental image editing skills. The right crop can transform a mediocre composition into a striking image. Whether you are preparing images for Instagram, LinkedIn, or YouTube, choosing the correct aspect ratio is essential.

Precision Crop Controls

Our image cropper gives you eight drag handles for pixel-perfect control. Resize the crop area freely or lock the aspect ratio to maintain consistent dimensions across multiple images.

Aspect Ratio Lock

Keep your crop proportional with built-in presets for Instagram (1:1), portrait (4:5), widescreen (16:9), and story (9:16). The lock button toggles freeform mode for custom dimensions.

Zoom and Pan

Zoom in for detailed adjustments and pan around the image to position the crop area exactly where you want it. Fine-tune your composition without losing resolution.

Export at Full Resolution

The cropped image exports at the exact pixel dimensions you defined -- no downscaling. Download as JPEG, PNG, or WebP for maximum flexibility.

Aspect Ratio Quick Reference
Ratio	Common Dimensions	Best For	Platform
1:1	1080x1080	Profile photos, square posts	Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook
4:5	1080x1350	Portrait feed posts	Instagram, Pinterest
16:9	1920x1080	Landscape video, thumbnails	YouTube, Twitter/X
9:16	1080x1920	Stories, Reels, Shorts	Instagram, TikTok, YouTube
2:3	1200x1800	Portrait photography	Pinterest, print
3:2	1800x1200	Landscape photography	Blog posts, articles
21:9	2560x1080	Ultrawide banners	Twitter header, desktop wallpaper
Cropping Best Practices
Follow the rule of thirds -- position key subjects along the grid lines for balanced compositions.
Avoid cropping too tightly around faces. Leave some breathing room for social media rounded corners.
Use the same aspect ratio for a series of posts to create a cohesive feed aesthetic.
For print, always crop at the final output resolution to avoid quality loss from upscaling.
Check platform guidelines -- each social network has specific optimal image dimensions.
Common Cropping Mistakes
Cropping at joints: Avoid cutting off limbs at the ankle, wrist, or knee -- it looks unnatural.
Too much headroom: Leaving too much space above the subject makes the image feel empty.
Ignoring orientation: A vertical crop for a horizontal layout wastes pixels and looks awkward.
Over-cropping: Removing too much context can make the subject unrecognizable or the story unclear.
Cropping for Different Platforms
Instagram feed: Crop to 1:1 (1080x1080) for square posts or 4:5 (1080x1350) for portrait posts that fill more screen space.
Instagram Stories / Reels: Use 9:16 (1080x1920) full-screen vertical format. Keep text within the top and bottom safe zones.
YouTube thumbnails: Crop to 16:9 (1280x720) with bold, centered subjects. Thumbnails drive click-through rates.
LinkedIn banners: The cover photo is very short (1128x191). Crop tight and keep text in the safe center zone.
Facebook link previews: Open Graph images display at 1200x630 (1.91:1). Crop your images to this ratio for clean link shares.
Composition Techniques
Rule of thirds: Position key elements along the grid lines (or at their intersections) for naturally balanced compositions.
Leading lines: Use natural lines in your image (roads, fences, architecture) to draw the viewer's eye toward the subject.
Symmetry and patterns: Centered compositions with symmetrical elements create visually striking images that work well in square formats.
Negative space: Leaving empty space around your subject creates focus and gives text overlays room to breathe in social media graphics.
Fill the frame: Get close to your subject. A tight crop often creates more impact than a wide shot with too much background.
Crop Images Privately

All image cropping happens locally in your browser. Your images never leave your device.

SquarePic
Free HD Image Upscaler

Upscale images 2x, 3x, or 4x with high-quality bicubic interpolation and smart sharpening. All processing is done locally in your browser.

Drop an image or click to browse

PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, GIF, TIFF — up to 30 MB

More Free Image Tools

Crop, convert, compress & resize - all in your browser.

Image Converter

JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF

Image Compressor

Reduce file size, batch

Image Cropper

Free-form & preset ratios

HD Image Upscaler

2x, 3x, 4x magnification

How to Upscale Images Without Losing Quality

Image upscaling enlarges a photo while minimizing quality loss. Unlike simple browser zoom or stretching, our tool uses high-quality bicubic interpolation followed by smart sharpening to produce crisp, usable results at 2x, 3x, or 4x the original size.

Bicubic Interpolation

Bicubic interpolation produces smooth, high-quality enlargements by sampling 16 surrounding pixels (a 4x4 grid) for each output pixel. It preserves edge sharpness better than bilinear filtering while avoiding the blocky artifacts of nearest-neighbor scaling.

Smart Sharpen (Unsharp Mask)

After upscaling, a subtle unsharp mask is applied to enhance edge contrast and recover detail that naturally softens during enlargement. Adjust the toggle to control the effect.

2x, 3x & 4x Scaling

Choose from three common magnification factors. 2x is ideal for most use cases, 3x for aggressive enlargement, and 4x for extreme upscaling where maximum detail recovery is needed.

100% Private & Local

Every pixel stays on your device. The entire upscaling process runs in your browser using the Canvas API — nothing is uploaded to any server.

Upscale Factor Reference
Scale	Megapixels (1 MP input)	Example Input	Example Output
2x	4 MP	1080 × 720	2160 × 1440
3x	9 MP	1080 × 720	3240 × 2160
4x	16 MP	1080 × 720	4320 × 2880
When to Upscale Images
Print enlargement: Upscale low-resolution photos before printing to avoid pixelation at larger print sizes.
Social media covers: Enlarge small images to fit banner dimensions for Twitter, LinkedIn, or Facebook without stretching.
Product photos: Increase resolution of product images for e-commerce platforms that require high-resolution uploads.
Thumbnails to heroes: Convert small thumbnails into larger hero images for blog posts and landing pages.
Legacy photo restoration: Enlarge old digital photos to modern resolution standards before editing or sharing.
Website hero images: Upscale stock photos or small graphics to fit full-width hero sections on landing pages without quality loss.
Presentation slides: Increase resolution of embedded images before inserting into slide decks to avoid pixelation on projectors or large displays.
Digital art portfolios: Prepare artwork at higher resolutions for print-on-demand services that require minimum dimension thresholds.
Upscaling Best Practices
Start with the highest quality source image available. Garbage in, garbage out.
Use 2x upscaling for the best quality-to-size ratio. 4x is best for small source images.
Always keep the Smart Sharpen toggle on unless you prefer a softer look.
Export to PNG for maximum quality, or WebP for smaller files with good quality.
For best results, upscale images that are already sharp and well-exposed.
Understanding Upscaling Quality
Bicubic interpolation produces smoother results than bilinear or nearest-neighbor by sampling 16 surrounding pixels. It preserves edge definition better than simpler algorithms.
Smart Sharpen applies an unsharp mask after upscaling to enhance edge contrast. This recovers some of the perceived detail that naturally softens during enlargement.
Upscaling is not magic — it cannot create detail that is not in the original image. The best results come from sharp, well-exposed source images. Severely compressed or blurry originals will not look sharp after upscaling.
Source quality matters: A 500x500 image upscaled 4x to 2000x2000 will look significantly better if the original was saved at JPEG quality 95% versus 60%.
When Each Scale Factor Works Best
2x upscaling: Best quality-to-size ratio. Use for most general-purpose enlargements — profile pictures, social media posts, and blog images. Results are crisp with minimal softening.
3x upscaling: Good for moderate enlargement needs. Use when you need to convert small thumbnails to medium-sized display images or prepare images for half-page print layouts.
4x upscaling: Maximum enlargement for extreme cases. Best for converting tiny images for large displays, full-page print, or when the source image is very small and no alternative exists.
Private & Secure Upscaling

All image upscaling happens locally in your browser using GPU-accelerated bicubic interpolation. Your images never leave your device.

Why Image Dimensions Matter
Consistent Brand Appearance

Each social media platform displays images at specific dimensions. Using non-standard sizes forces platforms to crop, stretch, or letterbox your images, resulting in an inconsistent brand appearance. A 1080x1080 square image displays perfectly across Instagram, Facebook, and LinkedIn feeds.

Faster Page Load Times

Uploading images at the exact display size eliminates unnecessary data. A 4000x3000 photo scaled down to 400x300 in the browser wastes bandwidth and slows page loads. Use the calculator above to find the exact dimensions for each platform, then resize to match.

Aspect Ratio Explained

Aspect ratio describes the proportional relationship between width and height (e.g., 1:1 for square, 16:9 for widescreen). Two images with different pixel dimensions can share the same aspect ratio. Use our calculator to find which platform presets match your image's aspect ratio.

Avoid Upscaling Issues

Starting with an image that is smaller than the target dimensions means the platform must upscale it, causing blurriness and pixelation. Always upload images at or above the platform's recommended resolution. Our dimension calculator shows you the minimum size for each media type.

How to Use the Image Size Calculator
Search by dimensions: Enter your image's width and height in pixels. The calculator instantly checks if these dimensions match any standard social media image size.
Browse by platform: Select a platform from the buttons above to see all supported image sizes for that platform, from profile pictures to cover photos and post dimensions.
Click through to resize: Once you find your target dimensions, click any result to open SquarePic's resizer with the exact preset applied.
Common pairings: 1080x1080 (Instagram square), 1080x1920 (Instagram Stories), 1200x630 (Facebook link preview), 1280x720 (YouTube thumbnail) -- these are among the most frequently searched dimension pairs.
Common Image Dimension Questions
What is the most common image size for social media?

1080 x 1080 pixels (1:1 square) is the most universally supported size. Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and X/Twitter all display square images natively. It is the safest choice for cross-platform posting.

How do I calculate aspect ratio from width and height?

Divide both width and height by their greatest common divisor. For example, 1920x1080 simplifies to 16:9 (1920/120 = 16, 1080/120 = 9). Use this calculator to find which standard aspect ratio matches your image dimensions.

What resolution is best for print vs web?

For web, 72 DPI is standard and 1920px on the longest side is sufficient for most displays. For print, 300 DPI is required. Use the dimensions above as a starting point and always verify with your specific platform's requirements before uploading.

Instagram Image Sizes: Complete Dimensions Guide

Instagram image sizes for posts, stories, profiles, and reels. Square posts are 1080x1080, portrait is 1080x1350, landscape is 1080x566.

320X320
1080X566
1080X1350
1080X1080
1080X1920
All Instagram Image Sizes
Profile Picture: 320 x 320 px

Aspect ratio: 1:1

Centering the subject in the square crop matters more than background detail.

Landscape Post: 1080 x 566 px

Aspect ratio: 1.91:1

Great for showing wide scenes like landscapes, cityscapes, and group shots.

Portrait Post: 1080 x 1350 px

Aspect ratio: 4:5

The most engaging format for Instagram feed. Takes up more vertical screen space.

Square Post: 1080 x 1080 px

Aspect ratio: 1:1

The classic Instagram format. Works well for all content types.

Stories: 1080 x 1920 px

Aspect ratio: 9:16

Leave 250px top and bottom clear of critical content for the safe zone.

Frequently Asked Questions
What is the standard image size for Instagram?

Instagram supports multiple image formats. The most common sizes are 320x320 pixels, 1080x566 pixels, 1080x1350 pixels. Use SquarePic to resize your photos to any of these exact dimensions.

How do I resize images for Instagram without cropping?

Use SquarePic's free image resizer. Upload your photo, select the Instagram preset that matches your needs, and choose Dynamic Blur or Solid Background mode to fill any empty space without cropping your original image.

Is Instagram image resizing free?

Yes. SquarePic is completely free with no signup required. All image processing happens locally in your browser using HTML5 Canvas. Your photos are never uploaded to any server.

What is the best image format for Instagram?

For Instagram, JPEG is best for photos with smooth gradients, PNG is ideal for graphics with text or sharp edges, and WebP offers excellent quality at smaller file sizes. SquarePic supports all three formats for export.

Can I create a Instagram profile picture with SquarePic?

Yes. Upload your photo to SquarePic and use our free editor to make it perfectly square. Choose the Instagram preset size and export a high-quality profile picture in seconds.

Best Practices for Instagram Images
Recommended Formats

JPEG is the standard for Instagram uploads. PNG preserves quality for graphics with text. WebP is supported but not recommended for maximum compatibility.

Quick Facts

Instagram applies its own compression to every upload and crops feed images to square thumbnails. Matching the recommended dimensions keeps your full image visible and avoids avoidable quality loss.

Upload Tips

Post consistently at 1080x1080 or 1080x1350 for feed posts. Use 1080x1920 for Stories and Reels. Avoid compressed artifacts by uploading the highest quality version within Instagram's 20 MB limit.

Why Dimensions Matter

Instagram crops images in feed to square thumbnails by default. Using the correct dimensions ensures your full image appears without unexpected cropping. Portrait 4:5 posts take up more vertical screen space than squares, giving your content more visibility.

Convert PNG to AVIF Online - Free

Convert your PNG images to AVIF format instantly. All processing happens locally in your browser - no uploads, no signup, no watermarks.

PNG
AVIF
Convert PNG to AVIF Now
About PNG and AVIF Formats
PNG

Portable Network Graphics - lossless format with transparency support.

Best for: Logos, screenshots, graphics with sharp text and transparency.· Supports transparency· Lossless

AVIF

AV1 Image Format - next-gen format with 50% better compression than JPEG.

Best for: Next-gen web performance, HDR content, highest compression needs.· Supports transparency· Lossy compression

Tips for Converting PNG to AVIF
AVIF offers 50% better compression than JPEG at the same quality level.
AVIF supports HDR, wide color gamut, and transparency.
Browser support is at 93% - provide a JPEG or WebP fallback for older browsers.
AVIF is ideal for serving high-quality images on modern browsers while minimizing bandwidth usage.
When to Convert PNG to AVIF
Next-generation image compression

PNG to AVIF conversion delivers 50% better compression than JPEG while maintaining transparency support. It is the most efficient format for modern websites targeting the best possible performance.

Who needs this: Forward-thinking web developers and performance teams building next-gen web experiences.
